ALPHABET = '123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz'
def b58(data):
    n = int.from_bytes(data, 'big')
    out = ''
    while n:

    zeros = len(data) - len(data.lstrip(b'\x00'))

title: Transaction Fees

nodes.label: Who pays the fee
nodes.body: The first section of the chapter explains that a transaction fee is a bid in an auction for the room in a block, that it is paid by the spender because only the spender's signature can commit to it, and that it is nothing but the gap between inputs and outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The subject is a good first lesson for a newcomer because it needs no special software: a calculation with two numbers explains it, and the node's refusals show the safeguards. In the study each statement of the section was checked on a private test chain of Bitcoin Core 31.1 and in a block of the real chain. This subject covers Fee as difference; Spender and signature; Miner choice.

nodes.label: Fee as difference
nodes.body: The first subject asks what a fee is on the level of the bytes: no field, only a gap between what goes in and what comes out, and the consequences for a sender who forgets a change output (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It matters because a transaction built by hand is the one place where a wrong subtraction costs real money, and because every wallet, explorer and estimator reads the fee the same way. This subject covers Fee is inputs minus outputs; Forgotten change becomes fee; No fee field in transaction.

nodes.label: Fee is inputs minus outputs
nodes.body: A Bitcoin transaction has no field called fee; the fee is whatever is left over when the values of all the outputs are subtracted from the values of all the inputs, and the miner who includes the transaction collects that remainder (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This matters because the person building a transaction has to account for every satoshi: the node can only check that the outputs do not exceed the inputs, and it cannot know what the sender meant to keep. Think of paying a shop bill with a banknote and walking away without waiting for the change; the difference is gone, and nobody can tell it was a mistake. In this study the 31.1 node of Bitcoin Core was started on a private test chain (regtest) and a transaction spent one 20-bitcoin output to make a payment of 1 bitcoin with no change output at all; an independent parser written for this chapter read the raw bytes of the transaction, summed the output values, and obtained 1,900,000,000 satoshis (19 bitcoins) as the difference, exactly the fee the node listed for the transaction in its mempool, the waiting room of unconfirmed transactions (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
nodes.definition: A transaction of one 20-bitcoin input and one 1-bitcoin output leaves 19 bitcoins (1,900,000,000 satoshis) unspent, and the node lists exactly that as the fee of the transaction in its mempool.

io.code: t = L.parse_tx(R['fee_arith']['tx']['hex']); out = sum(o['value'] for o in t['vout']); (round(R['fee_arith']['inputs_btc'] * 10 ** 8 - out), round(R['fee_arith']['mempoolentry_fees']['base'] * 10 ** 8), len(t['vin']), len(t['vout']))

nodes.label: Forgotten change becomes fee
nodes.body: A change output is the output that sends the unspent remainder of an input back to the sender; if it is left out, the remainder silently becomes fee, which the book illustrates with a 20-bitcoin output used for a 1-bitcoin payment so that 19 bitcoins would go to the miner (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nodes therefore carry a safety net: sendrawtransaction refuses by default any transaction whose fee rate is above DEFAULT_MAX_RAW_TX_FEE_RATE, a constant of COIN divided by 10 per kilo-virtual-byte (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like a bank that stops a transfer of an absurd amount until you confirm it. In the run the node answered testmempoolaccept with the reason max-fee-exceeded and sendrawtransaction with an error naming maxfeerate; the transaction was then submitted on purpose with that check switched off, mined in the next block, and the coinbase transaction of that block paid out 4,400,000,000 satoshis, the regtest subsidy of 2,500,000,000 plus the 1,900,000,000 that should have been change.
nodes.example: no change output on a 20 BTC input
nodes.definition: The node refuses the transaction that forgot its change with the reason max-fee-exceeded, and when the sender forces it through, the miner's coinbase pays out the subsidy plus the 19 bitcoins.

nodes.label: No fee field in transaction
nodes.body: The serialized transaction that nodes exchange contains a version, a list of inputs, a list of outputs, optional witness data and a lock time, and nothing else; the fee is never written into it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That design is deliberate and efficient: because the signature of every input commits to all the outputs, the spender commits to the fee without spending one extra byte of block space on a fee field, and any node can recompute the fee by looking up the values of the outputs being spent. It is the same as a receipt that lists only what was handed over and what came back, so that the shop's take is simply the gap. The chapter's own parser, written without Bitcoin Core code, split the 191-byte transaction of the run into its parts, found one input and one output, rebuilt the transaction identifier (txid) by hashing the serialization without witness data, and confirmed that it matched the node's identifier; no key called fee exists in the result (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: the fields of a parsed transaction
nodes.definition: Parsing the raw bytes of a transaction with an independent parser gives version, inputs, outputs, witness and lock time and no field called fee: the fee exists only as a difference.

io.code: t = L.parse_tx(R['fee_arith']['tx']['hex']); ('fee' in t, sorted(k for k in t if k in ('version', 'vin', 'vout', 'locktime')), t['txid'] == R['fee_arith']['tx']['txid'])

nodes.label: Spender and signature
nodes.body: The second subject asks who can pay a fee: the sender, because the signature covers the outputs, and the receiver only through a second transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It matters because the design explains why fee bumping comes in two kinds, one that only the sender can do and one that anyone who receives an output can do. This subject covers Fee needs the spender's signature; Fee paid in another transaction.

nodes.label: Fee needs the spender's signature
nodes.body: Because a signature commits to the outputs of a transaction, nobody can add to the fee of someone else's transaction, and a fee needs the spender's agreement; the book states that it is not possible for a transaction to pay a fee without the permission of the spender (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the run a signed one-input transaction was first checked with testmempoolaccept, the RPC that tests a transaction against the mempool rules without broadcasting it, and was allowed; the same bytes were then altered so that the first output was 5,000 satoshis smaller, which would have increased the miner's fee by 5,000 satoshis, and the node refused it with a script verification failure saying that the signature must be zero for failed CHECK(MULTI)SIG operation, which is the way the node reports that the signature no longer fits the changed data. A cheque works in the same way: if a stranger changes the amount after you have signed, the bank will not honour it. This is why fees are customarily paid by the spender and why a receiver who wants more speed must pay in a separate transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: an output lowered by 5,000 satoshis after signing
nodes.definition: A signed transaction is accepted by the node; the same transaction with its first output lowered by 5,000 satoshis (a larger fee) is refused because the signature no longer matches.

io.code: x = R2['tamper']; (x['original']['allowed'], x['tampered']['allowed'], x['tampered']['reject-reason'][:36], x['output0_original_sat'] - x['output0_tampered_sat'])

nodes.label: Fee paid in another transaction
nodes.body: A receiver of money cannot raise the fee of the transaction that paid them, but they can spend the output they received in a new transaction that pays a high fee; because that child can only be mined together with its parent, the miner is paid for both, which is the idea of child pays for parent (CPFP) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The fee is then paid in a different transaction than the one it helps. It is like a passenger who is stuck in a queue and pays the ferryman extra so that the whole line moves. In the run a parent paid 141 satoshis (1 satoshi per virtual byte) and its child 14,100 satoshis (100 per virtual byte); the block that the node assembled contained both, with the parent placed before the child as the rules of consensus demand, and the miner received 14,241 satoshis for the pair (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). This is the exception the book mentions when it says that the receiver of a transaction can pay a fee in a different transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: The receiver of an output can pay for the parent in a different transaction: the parent paid 141 satoshis, its child 14,100, and the node mined both together in one block.

nodes.label: Miner choice
nodes.body: The third subject asks who decides which transactions enter a block: the miner, who treats the fees as bids and fills a scarce space with the highest-paying transactions, and who alone may claim the subsidy in the coinbase (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It matters because everything in the chapter, from fee rates to carve-outs, is a way of speaking to that decision. This subject covers A fee is a bid; Coinbase is excluded.

nodes.label: A fee is a bid
nodes.body: The book explains that a transaction fee is not a price set by the protocol or by a miner but a bid in an auction for the limited space of a block, and that miners choose the set of transactions whose bids earn the greatest revenue (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's block assembler works that way: it takes groups of transactions in order of fee rate, the fee divided by the size, until the block weight limit is reached (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is the same as a market stall owner who fills a limited table with the goods that bring the most money per square centimetre. To test this the node was offered ten independent transactions of the same size with fees from 141 to 7,050 satoshis, that is 1 to 50 satoshis per virtual byte, in scrambled order, and its block template listed all ten sorted from the highest fee rate to the lowest, 50.0 first and 1.0 last; the ordering was recomputed by the chapter from the fee and weight that the template reports. The result is a single run on one node, and other miners may use other software or other rules, because only the block's validity is enforced by the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: ten transactions sorted by the node
nodes.definition: Ten transactions of one size and ten different fees were offered to a node and its block template listed them from the highest fee rate (50 satoshis per virtual byte) to the lowest (1 satoshi per virtual byte).

nodes.label: Coinbase is excluded
nodes.body: The first transaction of every block is the coinbase transaction, which creates the new bitcoins of the block subsidy and collects the fees of all the other transactions; it spends no earlier output, so it pays no fee and cannot be fee bumped, and the book therefore ignores it when it talks about transactions in this chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The sum it may claim is set by consensus: the subsidy of the block height plus the total of the fees, checked in the source function that connects a block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like the cashier's own till, which receives the takings of the day without having paid anyone. In block 840,000, mined on 2024-04-20 by the pool ViaBTC according to the explorer mempool.space, the first transaction has the coinbase marker in its input, the subsidy computed by the chapter for that height is 312,500,000 satoshis, the fees reported are 3,762,561,499 satoshis, and their sum, 4,075,061,499 satoshis, is exactly the block reward the explorer lists (Mempool Space, 2026).

nodes.label: Fees and fee rates
nodes.body: The second section teaches that the price of block space is the fee rate, which is the fee divided by the size, and that the size is measured in virtual bytes after the discount for witness data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also has to tell the user about the units, the guards against absurd fees and the minimum rates, which changed in release 30.0 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). The study recomputed the sizes with an independent parser and tried the minimum rates on a node. This subject covers Size and weight; Fee rate arithmetic; Minimum rates.

nodes.label: Size and weight
nodes.body: This subject asks in what unit the size of a transaction is measured, because a price per unit needs a unit: weight units and virtual bytes, with the discount for witness data and the limit of the block (Lombrozo et al., 2015). It matters because the same transaction has three sizes, in bytes, in virtual bytes and in weight units, and mixing them gives wrong fee rates. This subject covers Weight and virtual size; Block weight limit.

nodes.label: Weight and virtual size
nodes.body: Since segregated witness, the size of a transaction that matters for fees is its weight, in weight units: the bytes without witness data count four times and the witness bytes (the signatures) once, so weight is three times the base size plus the total size, and the virtual size in virtual bytes is the weight divided by four and rounded up (Lombrozo et al., 2015). It is like a post office that charges full price for the parcel and a quarter price for the packing paper. A one-input, two-output transaction of the run has 113 bytes without witness and 222 bytes with it; the chapter's parser computed 3 x 113 + 222 = 561 weight units and 141 virtual bytes, and both numbers equal what the node says when it decodes the same transaction (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This matters because block space and fees are counted in these units, and a wallet that estimated a fee from the plain byte length would overpay for the discounted witness bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A one-input, two-output P2WPKH transaction has 113 bytes without witness and 222 with it, so its weight is 3 x 113 + 222 = 561 weight units and its virtual size is 561 / 4 rounded up, 141 virtual bytes, as the node says.

nodes.label: Block weight limit
nodes.body: A block may weigh at most 4,000,000 weight units, a limit defined by BIP 141 and written in Bitcoin Core as the constant MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT, together with the witness scale factor of 4 (Lombrozo et al., 2015). Because the room in a block is finite, transactions compete for it, and that competition is what gives fees their value; it is the same as seats in a lift, where the operator prefers the passengers who pay the most for each seat taken. Block 840,000 weighed 3,993,281 weight units according to the explorer, which is 998,321 virtual bytes and 99.83 percent of the limit, so the block was full and the 3,050 transactions it contained had to be chosen from a longer queue (Mempool Space, 2026). The chapter recomputed the share from the numbers of the block record and read the constant from the source file at the pinned release, v31.1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
nodes.definition: A block may weigh at most 4,000,000 weight units (the constant MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT); block 840,000 weighed 3,993,281, which is 998,321 virtual bytes and 99.83 percent of the limit.

nodes.label: Fee rate arithmetic
nodes.body: This subject asks how the price of block space is computed and written: the division of the fee by the size, the units in which it is written, the mistakes between units and the guard against absurd amounts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It matters because a wallet is trusted with money and a wrong power of ten in a field is the commonest way to lose it. This subject covers Fee rate definition; Units of fee rate; Wrong unit factor; Absurd fee guard.

nodes.label: Fee rate definition
nodes.body: The fee rate is the price per unit of block space: the fee divided by the size of the transaction, in satoshis per virtual byte (sat/vB) or per weight unit; the book compares it to dividing the price of bags of rice by their weight to find the best deal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). One sentence of the printed book says the opposite, that the term fee rate is used for a transaction's size divided by weight, which gives a number without any price in it; the sentence is an error of wording that the book's later text and every wallet contradict, and it is not corrected in the development branch of the book repository either (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter computed it for a transaction of the run that paid 282 satoshis for 141 virtual bytes: the fee divided by the size is 2.0 satoshis per virtual byte, or 0.5027 per weight unit, while the size divided by the weight is 0.2513, a pure number that no miner could use to compare bids (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
nodes.definition: The fee rate is the fee divided by the size: 282 satoshis over 141 virtual bytes is 2.0 satoshis per virtual byte (0.5027 per weight unit), while the book's wording, size divided by weight, would give 0.2513, which is no price at all.

io.code: x = R['rbf']['t1']; (x['fee_sat'] / x['vsize'], round(x['fee_sat'] / x['weight'], 4), round(x['vsize'] / x['weight'], 4))

nodes.label: Units of fee rate
nodes.body: A fee rate can be written in several units: the book lists satoshis per virtual byte (the most common today), satoshis per weight unit, and bitcoin per kilo-virtual-byte, which is the unit Bitcoin Core uses in its RPC answers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Converting needs care, as between litres per hundred kilometres and miles per gallon. The book's example answer of estimatesmartfee is 0.00006570 bitcoin per kilo-virtual-byte; multiplied by 100,000,000 satoshis per bitcoin and divided by 1,000 bytes per kilo-byte it is exactly 6.57 satoshis per virtual byte, computed in the chapter with exact fractions, and the 31.1 node's own answer of the run, 0.00001225, is 1.225. The same arithmetic shows that one bitcoin per kilo-virtual-byte would be 100,000 satoshis per virtual byte, which is the size of the mistake that a user could make by writing a number in the wrong field (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Wrong unit factor
nodes.body: The book warns that a fee rate copied into a field with another denominator can overpay by a factor of 1,000, or by 100,000,000 if the numerator is changed as well, and that wallets should make such a mistake hard (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's wallet RPCs have two fields for the same idea, fee_rate in satoshis per virtual byte and feeRate in bitcoin per kilo-virtual-byte, and the run shows that the two are consistent: asking fundrawtransaction for fee_rate 10 and for feeRate 0.0001 produced the identical fee of 1,410 satoshis on the same transaction (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The same number 10 in the bitcoin field would mean 10 bitcoins per kilo-virtual-byte, and the node refused it because the coins to be spent could not cover such a fee; the factor between the two units is 10^8 / 10^3 = 100,000. This is like writing a distance in miles on a form that wants metres; the safety net is the wallet, not the number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The wallet accepts fee_rate in satoshis per virtual byte and feeRate in bitcoin per kilo-virtual-byte: 10 and 0.0001 give the identical fee of 1,410 satoshis, while the number 10 in the second field is refused.

nodes.label: Absurd fee guard
nodes.body: An absurd fee, in the book's words, is a fee rate far above what estimators expect to be needed for the next block, and wallets should make it hard to pay one by accident without forbidding it, because there are rare legitimate reasons (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core implements the guard for raw transactions as DEFAULT_MAX_RAW_TX_FEE_RATE, set to COIN divided by 10 per kilo-virtual-byte, which is 0.1 bitcoin per kilo-virtual-byte or 10,000 satoshis per virtual byte; the override is the argument maxfeerate (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It resembles the limit on a payment card that asks for a second confirmation. The transaction of the run that paid 19 bitcoins over 110 virtual bytes paid 17,272,727 satoshis per virtual byte, 1,727 times the guard, and the node refused it with max-fee-exceeded until the argument was changed. The guard is a policy of the node and not a rule of the network, so a miner would still accept such a transaction in a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Minimum rates
nodes.body: This subject asks how low a fee rate may be: the minimum that nodes relay, the minimum that the wallet accepts and the smallest output that is worth creating, the dust limit (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It matters because these floors are policies and not laws of Bitcoin, they change from release to release and they decide whether a presigned transaction can ever be broadcast. This subject covers Minimum relay fee; Wallet minimum fee; Dust threshold.

nodes.label: Minimum relay fee
nodes.body: The minimum relay fee rate is the lowest rate at which a node will accept a transaction into its mempool and pass it on, so that nobody can fill the memory of the network with free transactions; since release 30.0 its default and that of the incremental relay fee are 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). It is like a minimum stamp price for letters. The source constants DEFAULT_MIN_RELAY_TX_FEE and DEFAULT_INCREMENTAL_RELAY_FEE both read 100 in the unit of satoshis per kilo-virtual-byte, which is 0.1 per virtual byte (Bitcoin Core, 2026). On the regtest node, whose getmempoolinfo reports the same minimum, a 141-virtual-byte transaction needs 14.1 satoshis, so 15; the node refused 8 satoshis and 14 satoshis with min relay fee not met, giving the numbers 8 < 15 and 14 < 15 in its message, and accepted 15. The rate is a default of the software and not a rule of Bitcoin, so some nodes and miners have different ones, which is why a transaction that is below it may still be mined by a miner who accepts it directly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: At the default minimum relay fee of 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte a 141-byte transaction needs 15 satoshis: the node refused 8 and 14 with min relay fee not met, and accepted 15.

nodes.label: Wallet minimum fee
nodes.body: The wallet that builds transactions for the user has its own floor, set by -mintxfee and defaulting to DEFAULT_TRANSACTION_MINFEE of 1,000 satoshis per kilo-virtual-byte, that is 1 satoshi per virtual byte (Bitcoin Core, 2026). That is ten times the 0.1 that relaying nodes accept since release 30.0, so the wallet is more cautious than the network, like a shopkeeper who adds a margin to the wholesale price. The second regtest run asked the wallet's send RPC for rates of 0.5, 0.1 and 1 satoshis per virtual byte: it refused 0.5 and 0.1 with the message that the fee rate is lower than the minimum fee rate setting of 1.000 sat/vB and accepted 1, while the node's own getmempoolinfo reported a minimum relay rate of 0.1. A wallet that wants to use the new low rates must therefore have its setting changed too, while the release notes advise that the two relay settings, the minimum and the incremental fee rate, are changed together (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025).

nodes.label: Dust threshold
nodes.body: An output is called dust when spending it would cost more in fees than it is worth, and nodes refuse to relay transactions that create such outputs; at the default dust rate of 3 satoshis per byte the threshold is the output size plus the 67 bytes of a witness input, times 3 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A coin worth less than the cost of picking it up is not worth picking up. The chapter computed (31 + 67) x 3 = 294 satoshis for a P2WPKH output, (43 + 67) x 3 = 330 for a P2WSH output and (13 + 67) x 3 = 240 for a pay-to-anchor output, the values the Lightning specification lists (Lightning developers, 2026). On the regtest node outputs of 293, 329 and 239 satoshis were refused with the reason dust, and outputs of 294, 330 and 240 were accepted. Dust matters for fee bumping because the anchor outputs of channels are deliberately close to this limit, and release 29.0 made one exception, a zero-fee transaction with a single dust output that must be spent by its child (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025).

nodes.label: Fee estimation
nodes.body: The third section shows how a node estimates the fee rate that is needed for a transaction to confirm in a given number of blocks, from its record of the past, and how far the numbers of the real network can be compared (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The default mode of the estimator was changed in release 28.0 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024), and the study adds real data from two blocks of the chain. This subject covers Estimator mechanics; Fee market on mainnet.

nodes.label: Estimator mechanics
nodes.body: This subject asks how a node guesses the fee rate that is needed: from the record of the past, with thresholds, targets and a mode that was changed in release 28.0 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). It matters because the guess is the default behaviour of most wallets, and a user who understands its limits knows when to override it. This subject covers The estimatesmartfee call; Confirmation target limits; Estimator thresholds; Default mode economical.

nodes.label: The estimatesmartfee call
nodes.body: Because fees are bids in an auction, no one can know in advance which fee rate will be enough, but a full node can learn from the past: it notes when it first saw each transaction, in which block it was confirmed and what fee rate it paid, groups similar ones and reads off how many blocks transactions of a given rate usually waited (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core offers this as the RPC estimatesmartfee, and the book shows the call bitcoin-cli -named estimatesmartfee conf_target=144 answering 0.00006570 bitcoin per kilo-virtual-byte for 144 blocks, about one day. It is like a weather forecast made from the record of earlier days. A brand-new regtest node answered the same call with the error Insufficient data or no feerate found, because it had seen no history; after the chapter's script had made 120 blocks with 2,640 payments of mixed fee rates the node answered 1.225 satoshis per virtual byte for 2 blocks and 1.173 for 6 and 25 blocks. These numbers describe the artificial market of the test and say nothing about the real network, whose estimate on the day of the study could not be asked because no network node was run (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
nodes.definition: A fresh node answers the book's call with Insufficient data or no feerate found; after 120 blocks and 2,640 payments of mixed fee rates it answered 1.225 satoshis per virtual byte for 2 blocks and 1.173 for 6 and 25.

nodes.label: Confirmation target limits
nodes.body: The RPC takes a confirmation target in blocks from 1 to 1008, as its help text in the source says, but a target is only as good as the history behind it: the estimator keeps several time scales and the function MaxUsableEstimate limits the target to half the span of blocks it has seen, so that there are enough failing data points for the estimate to mean something (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A forecaster with two weeks of records cannot honestly promise a forecast for next year. On the test chain, which was 231 blocks high at the time, the call for the target 144 was answered with the field blocks equal to 60 instead of 144, so the answer states for which target it is valid, and the book's listing, which shows 144 returned as 144, is true only for a node with a long history (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet that asks for a long target must therefore read the blocks field of the answer and not assume that its wish was granted (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).

nodes.label: Estimator thresholds
nodes.body: The estimator does not average fees; it looks for the lowest fee rate bucket for which enough of the transactions that paid it were really confirmed within the target. In the header file of the estimator three constants state what enough means: more than 85 percent of the transactions of a rate must confirm within the target (SUCCESS_PCT), 60 percent within half the target (HALF_SUCCESS_PCT) and 95 percent within double the target (DOUBLE_SUCCESS_PCT) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is the same logic as a school that wants a grade to be passed by most pupils who studied that much, and not only by the average pupil. The book describes the method in words and does not give these numbers; the chapter read them from the saved source of release 31.1, and they explain why an estimate can be higher than the lowest fee that was ever confirmed in time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The conservative mode demands the double-target condition for longer time horizons in addition (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
nodes.definition: The estimator looks for the lowest fee rate at which more than 85 percent of the transactions were confirmed within the target (60 percent within half of it, 95 percent within double), constants of the source file.

nodes.label: Default mode economical
nodes.body: The estimator can answer in two modes, economical, which reacts quickly to recent data and so may give lower fee rates, and conservative, which also requires the longer horizon to agree and so gives higher and steadier ones. Release 28.0 changed the default mode of estimatesmartfee from conservative to economical, in the words of its notes expecting less overestimation, particularly for users of replace by fee (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). It is like choosing between today's forecast and the forecast that also respects the season. The source of release 31.1 shows the argument default economical (Bitcoin Core, 2026), and the run confirms it: at the targets 2, 6, 25 and 144 the default answer equals the economical answer, and at 144 blocks the economical estimate was 1.122 satoshis per virtual byte, the conservative one 1.173, and the default 1.122, so a program written for an older release that relied on the conservative default now receives lower numbers. Optech lists the change among its entries for fee estimation (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
nodes.definition: Since release 28.0 the default mode of estimatesmartfee is economical, not conservative: on the 31.1 node the default answer equals the economical answer at all four targets and differs from the conservative one at 144 blocks.

nodes.label: Fee market on mainnet
nodes.body: This subject asks what the market looks like in real data: two mainnet blocks 2.5 years apart, a public explorer's recommendation of today and an early study of how people paid fees (Mempool Space, 2026). It matters because the book's statements about the market were written at one moment, and the numbers show how far the market can move. This subject covers Block fee census; Recommended fees today; Revealed fee behaviour.

nodes.label: Block fee census
nodes.body: To see what fees look like on the real network, the chapter downloaded from the explorer mempool.space the first 600 transactions of two blocks and recomputed the fee rate of each as its fee divided by its weight over four, leaving out the coinbase: block 840,000, the fourth halving block of 2024-04-20, and block 971,489, mined on 2026-10-15 (Mempool Space, 2026). Within the 599 transactions that follow the coinbase, the median fee rate was 1,436.45 satoshis per virtual byte in the first block and 3.02 in the second, while the explorer's own median for the whole block is 200 and 1 satoshis per virtual byte; the sample is the first part of the explorer's list of the block, and the large difference of the medians shows that it is the better-paying part and not the whole block. It is like looking at the price tags on the first shelf of a shop. The census shows that fee levels differ by a factor of hundreds between times, which is why an estimator must always be fed with recent data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Recommended fees today
nodes.body: Public explorers publish fee recommendations that the book calls web-based fee estimation services (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On 2026-10-15 the endpoint of mempool.space answered with a fastest, half-hour, hour, economy and minimum fee of 1 satoshi per virtual byte each, which suggests that the blocks had spare room and that the lowest rate was enough (Mempool Space, 2026). Its record of average fees per block group over the last year contains 1,096 points, from 798,426 satoshis at the lowest to 8,098,275 satoshis at the highest, about a tenfold range in what miners were paid in fees on average per block. It resembles the fare of a taxi that is cheap at night and expensive in the rain. The numbers are a snapshot of one site on one day and not a property of Bitcoin; they illustrate the book's remark that demand can change and move the equilibrium of fees up or down (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). nodes.label: Revealed fee behaviour
nodes.body: Before the fee market could be studied as a market, someone had to look at what people really paid. Moeser and Boehme analysed the historical behaviour of Bitcoin users in paying fees, identified several regime shifts that are largely explained by changes in the default client software or by the actions of big intermediaries, and concluded that rules dominate ratio, a state that is sustainable only while fees remain negligible (Moeser and Boehme, 2015). Their table of transaction latency for June 2012 to May 2013 gives the median wait in seconds: 1,339 for 1,503 transactions that paid no fee, 600 for 5,735 transactions that paid 0.0005 bitcoin and 520 for 1,905 that paid 0.001, and ten percent of the zero-fee transactions waited almost four hours, 13,927 seconds. It is like finding the price of a service by watching what people really put into the basket and not by asking them. The chapter's check confirms that these numbers stand in the saved copy of the paper; it does not recompute them, because that would need the blockchain of 2012 and 2013 (Moeser and Boehme, 2015). This example reads moeser_boehme_2015_fees.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. nodes.label: Replace by fee (RBF)
nodes.body: The fourth section is about replacing a transaction by a conflicting one that pays more, the first of the two fee bumping methods, and it is the part of the chapter that has changed most: full replacement is now the default and its option has been removed (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024) (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). The study ran the rules on a node and reproduced the book's warning about paying twice. This subject covers Replaceable signal; Replacement rules; Replacement hazards.

nodes.label: Replaceable signal
nodes.body: This subject asks which transactions can be replaced: those that signal, as BIP 125 defined, or all, which is now the default since release 28.0, and the option that was removed in release 29.0 (Harding, 2015) (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). It matters because the book's statement that full replacement is disabled by default is the first one that is out of date, and because merchants who accept unconfirmed payments depend on the answer. This subject covers Opt-in signal rule (BIP 125); Signal in the wild; Full RBF by default; Removed option.

nodes.label: Opt-in signal rule (BIP 125)
nodes.body: Replace by fee (RBF) means that a node replaces a transaction in its mempool with a conflicting one that pays more. The version of the rule that Bitcoin Core introduced in release 0.12.0 was optional for the sender: a transaction signals that it may be replaced when at least one of its inputs has a sequence number below 0xfffffffe, as BIP 125 specifies (Harding, 2015), and release 0.12.0 listed it among its changes (Bitcoin Core developers, 2016). It is like a note on a parcel saying that the contents may be exchanged. The chapter's rule function gives true for 0xfffffffd, false for 0xfffffffe and 0xffffffff, and true for a transaction with several inputs when at least one signals; all 60 transactions that Bitcoin Core's wallet built in the run carried the single sequence 0xfffffffd, the value that signals while leaving the lock time active (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book calls opt-in RBF the signalling variant that has been default in Core for several years, and notes that a wallet only has to set a sequence number to use it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A transaction signals replaceability when at least one input has a sequence number below 0xfffffffe: 0xfffffffd signals, 0xfffffffe and 0xffffffff do not, and every transaction of Bitcoin Core's wallet in the run used 0xfffffffd.

nodes.label: Signal in the wild
nodes.body: If every wallet signalled, the signal would say nothing; the chapter therefore counted how many real transactions signal. Of the first 599 transactions after the coinbase of block 840,000, mined on 2024-04-20, 485 (81 percent) had an input with a sequence number below 0xfffffffe, and of the same number of block 971,489, mined on 2026-10-15, 273 (46 percent) did (Mempool Space, 2026). The share is large enough that merchants cannot treat the lack of a signal as a safe sign any more, but also shows that many wallets have no reason to set the signal now that nodes replace transactions without it; it is the same as a lock that half of the doors in a street no longer have. The count reads the sequence fields in the explorer's record and applies the BIP 125 rule of the preceding leaf (Harding, 2015). A sample of 599 transactions of two blocks cannot give a figure for the whole chain, and the book's statement that merchants can check the signal remains technically true but of lower value (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Full RBF by default
nodes.body: Full RBF means that any unconfirmed transaction can be replaced by a conflicting one that pays enough, with or without a signal. The book says that full RBF can be optionally enabled in Bitcoin Core but is disabled by default (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); this has changed. Release 24.0.1 added the option -mempoolfullrbf with default off (Bitcoin Core developers, 2022), and release 28.0 changed its default from 0 to 1 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). It is as if a shop that only exchanged goods in boxes marked exchangeable now exchanges any goods. On the 31.1 node getmempoolinfo reports fullrbf true; a transaction with the final sequence 0xffffffff, which does not signal, was replaced by a transaction that spent the same output and paid twice the fee, and the first transaction left the mempool. The change is the end of a long dispute between merchants who accepted unconfirmed payments and developers, told in the first story of this chapter, and it is the first of the book's statements that is out of date today (Todd, 2022).

nodes.label: Removed option
nodes.body: A configuration option that stays forever makes a policy look like a choice, so developers remove options once nobody benefits from switching them. Release 29.0 notes that, starting with 28.0, -mempoolfullrbf defaulted to 1, that with widespread adoption users no longer benefit from disabling it, and that the option has been removed (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). It is like taking the switch out of a lamp that always has to be on. A 31.1 node was started on purpose with -mempoolfullrbf=0 and stopped at once with the message Error parsing command line arguments: Invalid parameter -mempoolfullrbf=0 and exit code 1; a node that is told to run with the option the book describes does not start at all. This is an example of a change of default that is also a change of interface, and a script or a service file that still passes the option breaks after an upgrade (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025).
nodes.definition: Release 29.0 removed the option -mempoolfullrbf, and a 31.1 node started with -mempoolfullrbf=0 stops with Invalid parameter -mempoolfullrbf=0 and exit code 1.

io.code: o = R2['removed_option']; (o['exit_code'], 'Invalid parameter -mempoolfullrbf=0' in o['message'], L.has('core_relnotes_29.0.md', 'the `-mempoolfullrbf` startup option was set to default to `1`'))

nodes.label: Replacement rules
nodes.body: This subject asks what a replacement must pay: the absolute fee, the incremental fee, and the idea of the feerate diagram, together with the wallet command that does it all (Harding, 2015) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It matters because each rule is a defence against an attack on the bandwidth of the network, and the numbers can be tested on a node. This subject covers Conflict rule; Absolute fee rule; Incremental fee rule; Fee bump with wallet; Feerate diagram rule.

nodes.label: Conflict rule
nodes.body: Two transactions conflict when they spend at least one common output, because only one transaction can spend a given output in the valid chain; the book defines conflicting transactions this way and says that replacement means creating a conflicting version that pays a higher fee (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like two cheques drawn on the same banknote. The chapter built three versions of one payment: version 0 spends input A, version 1 spends A and B, and version 2 spends B and C, and checked conflicts with the definition: versions 0 and 1 conflict (they share A), versions 1 and 2 conflict (they share B), versions 0 and 2 do not. On the node, version 1 replaced version 0 in the mempool and version 2 then replaced version 1, so only version 2 was waiting, which is what the conflict rule predicts (Harding, 2015); the consequence of the pair 0 and 2 not conflicting is shown in the leaf about paying twice.
nodes.example: two payments that spend the same output
nodes.definition: Two transactions conflict when they spend a common output: version 1 (inputs A and B) conflicts with version 0 (input A) and replaced it in the mempool, and version 2 (inputs B and C) conflicts with version 1, but not with version 0.

io.code: h = R2['hazard']; i = h['inputs']; (L.conflict(i['v0'], i['v1']), L.conflict(i['v1'], i['v2']), L.conflict(i['v0'], i['v2']), h['v0_in_mempool_after_v1'], h['v1_in_mempool_after_v2'])

nodes.label: Absolute fee rule
nodes.body: A replacement must pay at least as much in total fee as all the transactions it throws out; BIP 125 requires that the replacement pays an absolute fee of at least the sum paid by the original transactions, and Bitcoin Core's policy document of release 31.1 still lists the rule with its reason, that only requiring a higher fee rate could allow an attacker to make a miner lose revenue (Harding, 2015) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like an auction in which a new bid must at least equal the old one in money and not only in percentage. On the regtest node a payment of 282 satoshis was replaced by one of 564, and then two more replacements of the second were tried: one paying 514 satoshis was refused with the message less fees than conflicting txs, and one paying the same 564 satoshis was refused with not enough additional fees to relay. The book mentions that Core requires a higher total fee and that developers wished to remove this requirement because of its side effects, which are the subject of the leaf on pinning by a large child (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A replacement must pay at least the absolute fee of what it replaces: a replacement with 514 satoshis was refused with less fees than conflicting txs, and one with the same 564 satoshis with not enough additional fees to relay.

io.code: x = R['rbf']; (x['lower_fee']['fee_sat'], 'less fees than conflicting txs' in L.reason(x['lower_fee']['result']), x['equal_fee']['fee_sat'], 'not enough additional fees to relay' in L.reason(x['equal_fee']['result']))

nodes.label: Incremental fee rule
nodes.body: A replacement must also pay for the bandwidth it costs the network: the extra fee over the replaced transactions must be at least the incremental relay fee times the replacement's own virtual size, which the policy document illustrates with 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte and a replacement of 500 virtual bytes, that must pay at least 50 satoshis more (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Without this rule an attacker could send endless replacements that each raise the fee by one satoshi, like a bidder who raises by a cent a thousand times. On the regtest node the first payment of 564 satoshis was replaced by a transaction of the same size, 141 virtual bytes, so the least acceptable fee was 564 + 15 = 579 satoshis (the chapter's function gives 579); 578 satoshis were refused with 14 satoshis of additional fee when 15 were needed, and 579 were accepted. The rule exists in BIP 125 and the incremental fee is a setting of the node that became 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte in release 30.0 (Harding, 2015) (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025).
nodes.definition: The replacement must also pay the incremental relay fee (0.1 satoshi per virtual byte, 15 satoshis for 141 bytes) on top: 578 satoshis were refused with 14 less than 15, and 579 accepted.

io.code: x = R['rbf']; (L.min_replacement_fee(564, 141), x['short_by_one']['fee_sat'], 'error' in x['short_by_one']['result'], x['exactly_enough']['fee_sat'], 'ok' in x['exactly_enough']['result'], x['incremental'])

nodes.label: Fee bump with wallet
nodes.body: A user does not have to build replacements by hand: the wallet RPC bumpfee creates the new version, reduces the change or adds inputs, signs it and sends it. The book advises developers to give users a fee-bumping interface that does all this work and asks only how much the fee rate should rise (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The wallet's source computes the least acceptable total fee as the old fee plus the incremental relay fee for the new size, the same rule as above (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like a lift button that asks only for the floor. In the run a two-input transaction of 208 virtual bytes paid 416 satoshis (2.0 satoshis per virtual byte) and signalled with the sequence 0xfffffffd on both inputs; bumpfee replaced it with a transaction of the same size paying 1,457 satoshis (7.0 per virtual byte) and the original left the mempool. This is the method that the book calls the efficient one, because the replacement is often no larger than the original (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The wallet's bumpfee RPC created the replacement itself: a 208-byte transaction at 2 satoshis per virtual byte (416 satoshis, signalling with 0xfffffffd) became one at 7 (1,457 satoshis) and the original left the mempool.

io.code: b = R['rbf']['bumpfee']; (b['orig_fee_sat'] / b['orig_vsize'], round(b['new_fee_sat'] / b['new_tx'], 2), b['orig_sequences'], b['orig_in_mempool_after'], L.has('core_src_wallet_feebumper.cpp', 'Min total fee is old fee + relay fee'))

nodes.label: Feerate diagram rule
nodes.body: Newer versions of Bitcoin Core judge a replacement by a more general idea than a higher fee rate: the feerate diagram, a curve that shows how much fee a miner collects as the block space used grows when the mempool is taken in the best order. A replacement is accepted only if the diagram after the replacement is strictly better, and the code says so in a comment of its function ImprovesFeerateDiagram (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like comparing two shopping routes by the whole receipt at every stage and not by one price. The rules numbered 3 and 4 of the older policy, the absolute fee and the incremental fee, are still listed in the policy document of release 31.1, with the marks that some of the older rules were removed (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The diagram is built from the ordered chunks of the cluster mempool that Daftuar and his coauthors describe (Daftuar et al., 2024). This leaf quotes the source and is checked only as a passage; no test of the run was designed to make a replacement fail this rule alone.
nodes.example: a replacement must improve the feerate diagram
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core 31.1 no longer asks only for a higher fee rate; its source requires that a replacement strictly improves the mempool's feerate diagram, the curve of cumulative fee against cumulative size.

nodes.label: Replacement hazards
nodes.body: This subject asks what can go wrong with replacement: a payee paid twice, a replacement made expensive by a big child, and an attack that cycles replacements (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It matters because these are the reasons for later designs such as version-3 transactions. This subject covers Three versions paid twice; Large child pin; Replacement cycling.

nodes.label: Three versions paid twice
nodes.body: The book warns that when a payment is replaced more than once, all versions must conflict with each other, or several of them can be confirmed and the receiver is paid twice. It gives the example of version 0 with input A, version 1 with A and B, and version 2 with B and C: a miner who saved version 0 can mine both it and version 2 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter ran this on the node. The payment was 0.4 bitcoin; versions 0, 1 and 2 were created, and a miner that kept version 0 was imitated by the generateblock RPC, which mines a raw transaction that need not be in the mempool. Block one contained version 0; version 2 was still valid and waiting, and block two contained it; the payee received 80,000,000 satoshis instead of the 40,000,000 asked. It is like paying a bill twice because the first receipt was not cancelled. The simple remedy of the book is that every replacement keeps all the inputs of the previous version (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: When version 0 (input A), version 1 (A and B) and version 2 (B and C) of one payment of 0.4 bitcoin were made, a miner that kept version 0 mined it and then version 2, and the payee received 0.8 bitcoin.

io.code: h = R2['hazard']; (h['payee_asked_sat'], h['payee_received_sat'], h['v2_in_mempool_after_v0_block'], 'ok' in h['mine_v0'], 'ok' in h['mine_v2'])

nodes.label: Large child pin
nodes.body: Transaction pinning is making a fee bump so expensive or so impossible that it fails. One kind arises from the rule of absolute fees: if Alice's payment is about 100 virtual bytes and Bob spends it in a child of 100,000, replacing Alice's payment needs a fee that also covers Bob's child, and at the same fee rate it costs 1,001 times what she paid in the first place (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a parked car that is boxed in by a lorry: moving it means paying for the lorry too. In the run a parent of 141 virtual bytes paid 705 satoshis, and a child of 90,012 virtual bytes was attached to it at 5 satoshis per virtual byte; a replacement at 6 satoshis per virtual byte was refused with less fees than conflicting txs, and the least replacement that the node accepted paid 450,780 satoshis, which is 639 times the original fee. Release 28.0 and BIP 431 limit this kind of pin for version-3 transactions, which a later leaf measures (Zhao, 2024).
nodes.definition: A payment of 100 virtual bytes with a child of 100,000 makes a replacement pay for 100,100 bytes, 1,001 times the original; in the run a 90,012-byte child raised the price of replacing a 705-satoshi parent to 450,780 satoshis, 639 times.

nodes.label: Replacement cycling
nodes.body: Replacement cycling is an attack on protocols with time limits, such as the hash time-locked contracts (HTLCs) of the Lightning Network, in which a payment must be claimed before a certain block. Mallory, who is the counterparty, repeatedly replaces Bob's claim transaction with one of her own and then removes her transaction in turn, so that Bob's claim is dropped from mempools and does not confirm in time, and she can steal the payment (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It is like a thief who pulls the document from the letterbox, every time just before the postman takes it. Antoine Riard described it on the mailing lists in October 2023 and Optech's newsletter 274 of 2023-10-25 summarised the attack and the mitigations that Lightning implementations deployed (Bitcoin Optech, 2023). This leaf reports a published claim; the chapter's check finds the passages in the saved copies, and the attack was not executed because it needs several peers with their own mempools while the study ran one node, so it is listed among the experiments not carried out.
nodes.definition: Replacement cycling lets a counterparty repeatedly replace and remove a victim's time-sensitive transaction so that it never confirms in time; the claim is the Optech text, found in the saved copies, and the attack itself was not executed.

nodes.label: Child pays for parent (CPFP)
nodes.body: The fifth and sixth sections of the chapter are about the second fee bumping method, child pays for parent, and about package relay that makes it work when the parent is too cheap to be kept (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In release 31.0 the mempool was rebuilt around clusters, which changes the limits that the book describes (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). The study ran packages, a chain of 65 transactions and a miner with a very small block. This subject covers Packages and mining; Package relay; Cluster mempool.

nodes.label: Packages and mining
nodes.body: This subject asks how a miner prices a transaction together with its unconfirmed ancestors, the idea behind child pays for parent, and when a child helps and when it does not (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It matters because it is the one method of fee bumping that a receiver can use. This subject covers Package fee rate; Child beats high rate transaction; Low fee child loses; Ancestor feerate mining.

nodes.label: Package fee rate
nodes.body: When a child spends an output of an unconfirmed parent, a miner who wants the child must also take the parent, so the sensible thing to price is the pair: the book calls it a package, with an aggregate size and aggregate fees, and the package fee rate is the total fee divided by the total size (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's policy document defines the package feerate as the total modified fees divided by the total virtual size of all transactions in the package (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like a lorry whose driver is paid for the whole load, the good and the poor parcels together. In the run a parent paid 141 satoshis and its child 14,100 satoshis; the node's mempool entries show a chunk (a group priced together) with the fee 14,241 satoshis and the weight 1,122 weight units, which is 280.5 virtual bytes and 50.77 satoshis per virtual byte, while the chapter's exact fraction with each transaction rounded up to 141 virtual bytes gives 50.5. The parent alone, at 1 satoshi per virtual byte, would have waited for a long time (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
nodes.example: a parent at 1 sat/vB and a child at 100
nodes.definition: A parent paying 141 satoshis and a child paying 14,100 form a package of 14,241 satoshis over 280.5 virtual bytes (1,122 weight units), 50.77 satoshis per virtual byte, the figure the node's chunk fields show, or 50.5 when each size is rounded up to 141.

io.code: e = R['ancestor_mining']['cpfp_wins']['mempoolentries']; f = e['P']['fees']['chunk'] * 10 ** 8; (round(f), e['P']['chunkweight'], round(f / (e['P']['chunkweight'] / 4), 2), float(L.package_rate([141, 14100], [141, 141])))

nodes.label: Child beats high rate transaction
nodes.body: Child pays for parent works because miners rank packages and not single transactions; since release 0.13.0, Bitcoin Core builds its block templates from the feerate of a transaction inclusive of its unconfirmed ancestors (Bitcoin Core developers, 2016). To see it the node was restarted with a very small limit on the block size, so that only two of three transactions fitted: an unrelated transaction A that paid 20 satoshis per virtual byte, a parent P that paid 1, and its child C that paid 100. Taken alone A has a higher rate than P, but the package of P and C paid about 50.8, so the next block contained P and C, in that order because a parent must precede its child, and not A; the block weighed 2,014 weight units in all. It resembles a taxi dispatcher who takes the pair of passengers that together pay most. The test is a single run with an artificial limit on the block size and shows the ranking rule, not the real mix of the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: the pair at 50.8 comes before a lone transaction at 20
nodes.definition: In a block with room for two of the three transactions, the node chose the parent and its child (package rate 50.8) before an unrelated transaction paying 20 satoshis per virtual byte, and the parent comes before the child in the block.

io.code: a = R['ancestor_mining']['cpfp_wins']; b = a['block_txids']; t = lambda k: a[k]['txid']; (t('P') in b, t('C') in b, t('A') in b, b.index(t('P')) < b.index(t('C')), a['block_weight'])

nodes.label: Low fee child loses
nodes.body: A child does not always help: it must lift the average of the package above the competitors. In the second scenario of the run the child paid only 5 satoshis per virtual byte, so the package of parent and child paid 846 satoshis for 280.5 virtual bytes, 3.02 per virtual byte, below the 20 of the unrelated transaction A. The block with the same artificial limit contained A, and the parent and its child stayed in the mempool unconfirmed, which shows that the miner's rule is a comparison of rates and that a small tip on a stuck parent can be wasted. It is like adding a one-coin tip to a long taxi fare: it changes the average very little. The book makes the same point when it says that the miner sorts the transactions and packages by fee rate and includes the highest-revenue ones up to the maximum weight (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet that wants to bump with a child should therefore compute the child's fee from the package rate it needs and not from a fixed amount (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
nodes.example: a child at 5 sat/vB does not help
nodes.definition: With a child paying only 5 satoshis per virtual byte the package rate is 3.0, below the 20 of the unrelated transaction, which was mined alone while the parent and child stayed in the mempool.

io.code: a = R['ancestor_mining']['cpfp_loses']; b = a['block_txids']; t = lambda k: a[k]['txid']; (round((a['fees_sat']['P'] + a['fees_sat']['C']) / (a['mempoolentries']['P']['chunkweight'] / 4), 2), t('A') in b, t('P') in b, t('C') in b)

nodes.label: Ancestor feerate mining
nodes.body: Ancestor fee rate mining means that a miner looks at each transaction together with all of its unconfirmed ancestors, evaluates them as one package and can take them into the block as one unit; the book says that Core has done this for many years and that it is believed that almost all miners use it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Release 0.13.0 introduced it as an algorithm that selects transactions by their feerate inclusive of unconfirmed ancestor transactions (Bitcoin Core developers, 2016). In release 31.0 the same idea lives in the cluster mempool, where the unit is the chunk, a part of the best ordering of a cluster (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In the mempool entries of the run, the parent's chunk fee equals the child's ancestor fee, and both chunks weigh 1,122 weight units, so the node's own bookkeeping treats the two transactions as one unit of 14,241 satoshis. It is like a bus fare shared by a group, where the conductor wants the group that pays most for its seats.
nodes.example: chunk fee equals the child's ancestor fee
nodes.definition: Since release 0.13.0 miners rank transactions with their unconfirmed ancestors; in the 31.1 node the parent's chunk fee equals the child's ancestor fee, and both chunks weigh 1,122 weight units.

nodes.label: Package relay
nodes.body: This subject asks how a parent that is too cheap to be relayed can be helped by its child: by sending them together, with the RPC submitpackage, the relay of one parent and one child, and the message with which a peer names its minimum (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). It matters because the book says that package relay is the solution to a critical problem and that a limited early version may be available. This subject covers The minimum relay problem; The submitpackage RPC; One parent one child; The feefilter message.

nodes.label: The minimum relay problem
nodes.body: Child pays for parent has a hole: if the parent pays less than the minimum relay fee, a node will not keep it, and so the child that arrives later is an orphan whose parent is not known; the book calls this the minimum relay fee rate problem and says that package relay solves it, by letting nodes evaluate the fee rate of the whole package before deciding on any single transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a letter whose stamp is too cheap: the post office rejects it at the counter, though a second stamp is in your pocket. In the run a version-2 parent paid 8 satoshis for 141 virtual bytes, below the 15 needed; testmempoolaccept refused it alone with min relay fee not met, 8 < 15, a child alone was refused as spending a missing output, and the RPC submitpackage accepted both as a package, because the child's fee of 10,400 satoshis paid for the pair. This is the behaviour that release 31.0 extended from version-3 parents to all parents of a package with one parent and one child (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
nodes.example: a parent of 8 satoshis that no node would take alone
nodes.definition: A parent paying 8 satoshis (below the 15 needed) was refused alone with min relay fee not met, a child alone was refused as spending a missing output, and the two together were accepted by submitpackage.

nodes.label: The submitpackage RPC
nodes.body: The RPC submitpackage, which began as an RPC for the test network only and was opened to the other networks in 2023, hands a list of related transactions to the node to be validated and accepted together; the policy document says that packages must be child-with-parents, a child and at least one of its unconfirmed parents, and that a package is limited to 25 transactions (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). In release 28.0 the notes tell users to use it to send packages directly and let a version-3 parent be below the minimum relay feerate, even free (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). It is like handing in an application with all its attachments in one envelope. In the run a zero-fee version-3 parent of 123 virtual bytes and a child of 151 virtual bytes paying 10,000 satoshis were accepted with the message success; each result reports the same effective feerate of 0.00036496 bitcoin per kilo-virtual-byte, which is 36.5 satoshis per virtual byte over 274 virtual bytes. Alone, the parent was refused with min relay fee not met, 0 < 13.
nodes.example: a zero-fee version-3 parent with its anchor child
nodes.definition: The RPC submitpackage accepted a version-3 parent paying nothing together with a child paying 10,000 satoshis for both, an effective rate of 36.5 satoshis per virtual byte over 274 virtual bytes.

nodes.label: One parent one child
nodes.body: A node cannot always be handed a package by the user; the aim of package relay is that nodes pass packages to each other. Release 28.0 delivered a limited form: a transaction whose fee rate is too low is opportunistically paired with its child and submitted as a package, so that nodes can download one-parent-one-child packages with the existing relay protocol (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). Release 31.0 allows the parent of such a package to pay even nothing when it is not a version-3 transaction, and notes that further unconfirmed parents of the child must already be in the mempool (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). It is like a shop that accepts a coupon only when the product comes with a paying item. The book's prediction that a limited early version may be available at the time of publication has therefore come true, while the general package relay of BIP 331, which lets nodes ask for the ancestors of a transaction, is still a proposal (Zhao, 2022). The relay between nodes was not tested in this study, which ran a single node.
nodes.definition: Release 28.0 pairs a transaction whose fee rate is too low with its child and submits them as one package, and release 31.0 lets the parent of such a one-parent-one-child package pay nothing even when it is not version 3.

This expands the change from 28.0 to also cover packages of non-TRUC transactions'), L.has('core_doc_policy_packages.md', 'MAX_PACKAGE_COUNT=25'))

nodes.label: The feefilter message
nodes.body: Nodes protect their memory with a minimum fee rate, and BIP 133 added the message feefilter to tell the peers about it: a node instructs its peers not to send it announcements, called inv messages, for transactions with a fee rate below the one it names, which saves the bandwidth on both sides (Morcos, 2016). It is like telling the paper boy not to bring the free leaflets. The book's chapter on the network prints a peer listing in which the field minfeefilter is 0.00000000, a peer that asks for everything (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Release 0.13.0 notes the message among its changes and the effect on relaying below the filter feerate (Bitcoin Core developers, 2016). The reason it belongs to this chapter is that a low-fee parent that the peers filter out may never reach the miners, which is why the relay of a package as a whole has to be thought together with these filters. The study did not run a second node, so the message itself was not observed; the leaf is checked as a passage in the saved BIP and the saved chapter.
nodes.example: a peer says: send me nothing below this rate
nodes.definition: BIP 133 lets a node tell its peers the lowest fee rate it will accept so that they do not announce cheaper transactions, and the book's getpeerinfo listing shows the field minfeefilter of a peer as 0.

nodes.label: Cluster mempool
nodes.body: This subject asks how the mempool is organised in release 31.0: in clusters of at most 64 transactions, ordered into chunks, replacing the old limits of 25 related transactions (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). It matters because the numbers and the sentence about a day's worth of transactions in the book no longer describe the software. This subject covers Cluster limits; Chunks and linearization; Removed ancestor limits; Mempool size and expiry.

nodes.label: Cluster limits
nodes.body: In release 31.0 Bitcoin Core replaced the old mempool with the cluster mempool: transactions that are linked through parents and children form a cluster, and the default policy limits a cluster to 64 transactions and 101,000 virtual bytes (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). A small number of transactions per cluster limits the work needed to order them again each time something changes, which the old limits of 25 related transactions tried to do in a coarser way. It is like a library that limits each shelf to a size that one person can sort quickly. The source constant DEFAULT_CLUSTER_LIMIT is 64 and getmempoolinfo of the node returned limitclustercount 64 and limitclustersize 101000; a chain in which each payment spent the output of the one before was sent until it was refused: 65 were attempted, 64 accepted, and the 65th was refused with too-large-cluster (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The Optech topic page describes the design (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).

nodes.label: Chunks and linearization
nodes.body: A cluster is a connected component of the graph of mempool transactions; a linearization is an order of its transactions in which every parent comes before its children, and the aim is an order in which the best subset of the cluster comes first, then the best of the rest, and so on; these subsets are the chunks, whose feerates fall from one chunk to the next (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Daftuar and his coauthors propose that the sorted clusters are merged so that block building selects from the best chunks and eviction removes the set that would be selected last (Daftuar et al., 2024). It is like sorting a cupboard so that the most valuable items are in front, while keeping the boxes that are stacked together. In the run the parent paid 1 satoshi per virtual byte and its child 100: the node placed both in one chunk of 1,122 weight units, the sum of the two weights of 561, with a chunk fee equal to the sum of the two fees. The node reports these values in its mempool entries as the fee field chunk and the field chunkweight, and the terminology document of release 31.1 defines the weight fields (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: A cluster is linearized (put in an order that keeps parents before children) so that the highest fee rate prefix, a chunk, comes first; the parent and child of the run formed one chunk of 1,122 weight units.

nodes.label: Removed ancestor limits
nodes.body: Before release 31.0 Bitcoin Core refused to keep a transaction that would make more than 25 related transactions, or more than 101,000 virtual bytes of them, in its mempool; the book states the limits as 25 ancestors or descendants and 100,000 virtual bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and the notes of release 0.19.0.1 give 25 descendants and 101,000 virtual bytes (Bitcoin Core developers, 2019). Release 31.0 states that the mempool no longer enforces ancestor or descendant size and count limits and uses the cluster limits instead (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). It is as if a speed limit had been replaced by a limit on the size of the whole convoy. In the run a chain of 26 transactions, each spending the output of the one before, was accepted, which the old rule would have refused at the 26th, and 64 were accepted in all. Two things in the book's description are therefore out of date for release 31: the numbers were wrong by 1,000 virtual bytes, and the limits no longer exist.

nodes.label: Mempool size and expiry
nodes.body: The mempool is the memory in which a node keeps the transactions it has not yet seen confirmed. The book says that later versions of Bitcoin Core limited its size to hold about one day's worth of transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The constants of release 31.1 give two limits that are not about days: DEFAULT_MAX_MEMPOOL_SIZE_MB is 300 megabytes, and DEFAULT_MEMPOOL_EXPIRY_HOURS is 336 hours, which is 14 days, so that a transaction that was not mined is forgotten after two weeks (Bitcoin Core, 2026); the regtest node reports maxmempool 300,000,000 bytes. The book also says that the mempool keeps only the transactions or packages with the highest fee rate, so how long a transaction stays depends on the fee market and not on a clock; the sentence about a day is a rough picture and does not match the numbers in the code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It resembles a lift lobby with a fixed number of seats: how long a person waits depends on who else arrives (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: The default mempool holds 300 megabytes (-maxmempool) and forgets transactions after 336 hours, which is 14 days; the book's summary 'about one day's worth' describes neither number.

nodes.label: Pinning and anchors
nodes.body: The seventh and eighth sections of the chapter describe transaction pinning, in which the rules that protect nodes also make fee bumping impossible, and the carve-out and anchor outputs, which were made for Lightning (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Version-3 transactions and pay-to-anchor outputs are the newer solutions, and the carve-out has been removed in release 31.0 (Zhao, 2024) (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). The study ran each of the newer rules on a node. This subject covers CPFP carve out; TRUC policy; Anchor outputs.

nodes.label: CPFP carve out
nodes.body: This subject asks what the carve-out was: a 2018 exception to the descendant limits for Lightning, its real size, the quadratic reasoning behind the limits and its removal in release 31.0 (Corallo, 2018). It matters because the book teaches it as a present rule and the numbers it gives differ from the code. This subject covers Carve out rule; Carve out removed; Quadratic work.

nodes.label: Carve out rule
nodes.body: In 2018 Matt Corallo proposed an exception to the descendant limits for protocols such as Lightning, in which two parties sign transactions long before they are broadcast: one extra child of the transaction may be added even when the limit is reached, so that a malicious counterparty cannot fill the space and block the other from bumping the fee (Corallo, 2018). His message of 2018-11-29 proposed that this extra transaction be of size no greater than 1K in virtual size; the rule was merged as pull request 15681 and released in 0.19.0.1, where the notes say that one extra descendant is allowed provided that it is an immediate child and its size is 10,000 virtual bytes or less (Bitcoin Core developers, 2019). The constant of release 31.1 still bears the name EXTRA_DESCENDANT_TX_SIZE_LIMIT and equals 10000 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book says the extra transaction may be up to 1,000 virtual bytes and the total up to 100,000, the first being the number of the proposal and the second a rounding of the 101,000 of the code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); it is like quoting a price from the catalogue and not from the till. The chapter found all these texts in the saved sources. This example reads ml_corallo_2018-12_carveout.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: ('10000', True, True, True)

nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core's carve-out admitted one extra child of at most 10,000 virtual bytes beyond the 25-descendant and 101,000-byte limits (the constant is EXTRA_DESCENDANT_TX_SIZE_LIMIT of 10000), where the book says 1,000 and 100,000; Corallo's 2018 proposal had said 1K.

nodes.label: Carve out removed
nodes.body: The carve-out was a patch on top of the descendant limits, and when release 31.0 replaced those limits by cluster limits, the patch had nothing to attach to. The release notes say that the CPFP Carveout has been removed from the mempool logic, and that nothing is allowed to bypass the cluster count limit; the notes expect that smart-contract uses that need similar functionality will employ TRUC transactions and sibling eviction instead (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). It is as if a fire exit that had been added to a building was not needed after the building was redesigned. This is a change that the book could not foresee, but the book's text on the carve-out, which is a section of the chapter, now describes a rule of releases 0.19.0.1 to 30 and not of 31 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Optech's topic page still describes the carve-out as a relay policy implemented in Bitcoin Core and lists the later developments (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). The chapter found the removal in the saved notes and did not run it on a node of an older release.
nodes.definition: The carve-out was removed from the mempool in release 31.0 because the cluster limits replaced the descendant limits it worked around.

nodes.label: Quadratic work
nodes.body: The old limits were not arbitrary; the book explains that they protect the node from work that grows with the square of the limit. If a child pays for 25 ancestors and each of the ancestors has 25 other children, then including the package in a block requires updating about 625 packages, and doubling the parameter from 25 to 50 would quadruple the work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's arithmetic gives 25 x 25 = 625, 50 x 50 = 2,500 and the factor 4. It is like a handshake round in a room: with twice the people there are four times as many pairs to greet. The same reasoning drives the cluster mempool, whose limit of 64 transactions per cluster is set so that the ordering work of a cluster stays small (Daftuar et al., 2024). The lesson for a designer is that every limit in a peer-to-peer system is a trade between the freedom of the users and the work that an attacker can make the nodes do.

nodes.label: TRUC policy
nodes.body: This subject asks how version-3 transactions solve the problems of pinning: one parent, one child, small sizes, sibling eviction and a bound on the cost of a replacement (Zhao, 2024). It matters because it is the replacement of the carve-out in the new software. This subject covers TRUC limits; TRUC sibling eviction; TRUC version mixing; TRUC pinning bound.

nodes.label: TRUC limits
nodes.body: Topologically restricted until confirmation (TRUC) transactions, also called version 3 transactions, are an opt-in set of rules from BIP 431: a version-3 transaction may have at most one unconfirmed parent and one unconfirmed child, may be at most 10,000 virtual bytes, and its child at most 1,000 (Zhao, 2024). A version-3 transaction also signals replaceability even without the BIP 125 signal, and the unconfirmed relatives of a version-3 transaction must all be version 3 (Zhao, 2024). The aim is that a replacement can never be made very expensive by a large attached child. It is like a parking space that can hold one car and one trailer of limited size. The source constants of release 31.1 are TRUC_VERSION 3, TRUC_ANCESTOR_LIMIT 2, TRUC_MAX_VSIZE 10000 and TRUC_CHILD_MAX_VSIZE 1000 (Bitcoin Core, 2026), where the limit of two counts the transaction itself and one relative. In the run a version-3 parent had a child of 141 virtual bytes, which was accepted, and a child of 1,350 virtual bytes, which was refused with the message TRUC-violation, version=3 child tx; release 28.0 introduced the policy (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024).
nodes.definition: A version-3 (TRUC) transaction may have one unconfirmed parent and one child, at most 10,000 virtual bytes itself and 1,000 for the child; a child of 1,350 virtual bytes was refused, a child of 141 accepted.

nodes.label: TRUC sibling eviction
nodes.body: Because a version-3 parent may have only one unconfirmed child, a second child that arrives could be blocked by the first one, so the rule lets the second child replace the first, called sibling eviction, if it pays more: the replacement must pay a higher fee than the sibling it evicts (Zhao, 2024). It is like a single seat that goes to the highest bidder, though not to a bidder who only matches the first. In the run the first child was accepted; a second child of the same parent at the same fee rate was refused with the message insufficient fee including sibling eviction, and a second child at a higher fee rate was accepted and the first child left the mempool. For Lightning this means that one party cannot permanently occupy the single place beside the commitment transaction with a cheap child, which is the pinning that the carve-out tried to prevent (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
