nodes.label: TRUC version mixing
nodes.body: The rules of version 3 bind both sides: a version-3 transaction can only spend unconfirmed outputs of other version-3 transactions, and any other transaction can only spend an unconfirmed output of a version-3 parent if it is itself of version 3 (Zhao, 2024). It is like a club in which a member may only bring a guest who has signed the same rules. In the run a version-2 transaction that spent an unconfirmed output of a version-3 parent was refused with the message TRUC-violation, non-version=3 tx followed by its identifier, so a parent that opts in to the restrictions cannot be pinned by a child that did not. The restriction lasts only until confirmation, which is the origin of the name, and after that the output can be spent by anyone with any version (Zhao, 2024) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: A version-2 transaction that spends an output of an unconfirmed version-3 transaction is refused with TRUC-violation, because the rules bind both sides.

nodes.label: TRUC pinning bound
nodes.body: Pinning by a large child is bounded under the TRUC rules because the child cannot be larger than 1,000 virtual bytes, so the extra fee that a replacement must pay is bounded too; BIP 431 says that restricting children to 1000 virtual bytes lowers the upper bound of the added fees by a factor of 100 compared with a child of 100,000 (Zhao, 2024). The run repeated the pin of the earlier leaf with a version-3 parent of 141 virtual bytes that paid 705 satoshis and a child of 885 virtual bytes that paid 4,425 satoshis; the replacement that the node accepted had to pay 5,145 satoshis, against the 450,780 satoshis of the version-2 case, about 88 times less. It is like a lorry replaced by a small trailer in the example of the parked car. The numbers are a single run with one child size, and the bound of the specification is a factor of 100 in general (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).

nodes.label: Anchor outputs
nodes.body: This subject asks how a transaction that is signed long before it is sent can still be fee bumped: with an output that anyone can spend, the pay-to-anchor script, and the allowance of one dust output without fee (Sanders, 2025). It matters because Lightning channels are exactly this kind of presigned transaction. This subject covers Pay to anchor (P2A); Ephemeral dust; Anchor spend; Lightning anchor outputs.

nodes.label: Pay to anchor (P2A)
nodes.body: A pay-to-anchor (P2A) output is a small output with a standard script that anyone can spend: it is a segregated witness output of version 1 with the two-byte program 0x4e73, so the script is 51024e73, and it needs no signature, which makes it a handle for a child transaction to fee bump a parent (Sanders, 2025). It is like a hook on a wall that anyone can hang a rope on. The chapter parsed the zero-fee parent of the run and found its first output with exactly this script and the value 0; the address of such an output on the test chain is bcrt1pfeesnyr2tx, and the node refused a P2A output of 239 satoshis as dust and accepted one of 240. BIP 433, the specification, defines the type as an output with the script OP_1 followed by the push of 4e73 (Sanders, 2025). BOLT 3 lists a shared anchor output for commitments without fees, and the output needs no key, so it can be created long before it is spent (Lightning developers, 2026) (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
nodes.definition: The pay-to-anchor output is the witness version 1 program 0x4e73, the script 51024e73, and anyone can spend it; the run's anchor output carried exactly that script and the value 0.

nodes.label: Ephemeral dust
nodes.body: Ephemeral dust is the rule that makes a zero-fee anchor possible. Dust outputs are normally not relayed; release 29.0 allows one dust output in a transaction provided that the transaction pays no fee, and requires that any spender of its other outputs also spends the dust, so that the dust cannot stay in the set of unspent outputs (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). It is like a free sample that must be taken away by whoever buys anything else from the stand. In the run the zero-fee version-3 parent had an anchor output of value 0: alone it was refused with min relay fee not met, 0 < 13, together with its child it was accepted, and after mining the mempool was empty, so the dust was spent in the same block. The source file of the policy explains the safety conditions of its functions, and Optech's page on ephemeral anchors shows the history (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). The book mentions ephemeral anchors as a proposal that is being developed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Anchor spend
nodes.body: Spending the anchor shows why the construction fits a time-sensitive contract: the child has two inputs, one for the money that pays the fee and one for the anchor; the anchor input has an empty witness, because the output needs no signature, and the child paid 10,000 satoshis from a 1-bitcoin input. The chapter parsed the child's raw bytes and found two inputs and exactly one with an empty witness stack. Whoever sees the parent, the counterparty or a third party, can attach a child like this, and that is the strength of the anchor and also the reason for the careful limits, because an anyone-can-spend handle invites competition (Sanders, 2025). It is like a tow rope on a car that any helper may take, with the rule that only one rope may be attached. The version-3 rules of the previous leaves make sure that only one child can occupy the place of the anchor spend (Zhao, 2024).

nodes.label: Lightning anchor outputs
nodes.body: The Lightning Network keeps payments between two parties in channels, whose commitment transactions are signed in advance and may be broadcast at an unknown time; the book says that most popular implementations use a template called anchor outputs, designed to be used with the carve-out (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the specification of the commitment transaction, BOLT 3, the anchor output of each party is fixed at 330 satoshis, the default dust limit for P2WSH, and after 16 blocks anyone can sweep it, so that the outputs do not stay for ever in the set of unspent outputs (Lightning developers, 2026). It is like a small deposit on a trolley that is returned when someone takes it back. Optech's page records that later designs came to depend on the carve-out to circumvent pinning and that the newest designs differ (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). The specification also lists the dust limit of 240 satoshis for the pay-to-anchor type, and the chapter found these passages in the saved copies; the protocol itself was not run.

nodes.label: Fee sniping and incentives
nodes.body: The ninth and tenth sections of the chapter are about adding fees correctly and about the defence against fee sniping with the lock time, which only matters when fees are a large part of the miner's income (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The study computed the subsidy and the fee share of real blocks, measured the lock times of a wallet and of the chain, and found that the book's example of the lock time is off by one block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Block reward mix; Sniping attack; Lock time defense against fee sniping.

nodes.label: Block reward mix
nodes.body: This subject asks what part of a miner's income are fees: the subsidy and its halvings, the fee share of two real blocks and the arguments about a future of fees only (Nakamoto, 2008). It matters because the defence against fee sniping is only needed when fees are large. This subject covers Subsidy halvings; Fees versus subsidy; A future with fees only.

nodes.label: Subsidy halvings
nodes.body: The block subsidy is the amount of new bitcoin that the miner of a block may create in its coinbase transaction; it started at 50 bitcoins and is cut in half every 210,000 blocks, which the book describes in its chapter on mining as 6.25 new bitcoins in 2023 and a coming halving at block 840,000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the source function GetBlockSubsidy the rule is a shift: the number of halvings is the height divided by 210,000, the starting value is 50 coins, and the value is shifted right by the number of halvings (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like a pie that is cut in half at every anniversary. The chapter's function gives 5,000,000,000 satoshis at the heights 0 and 209,999, 2,500,000,000 at 210,000, 625,000,000 at 839,999 and 312,500,000 at 840,000 and at the height 971,489 of 2026-10-15. The subsidy matters for this chapter because every halving makes the fees a larger part of what a miner earns (Nakamoto, 2008).
nodes.definition: The subsidy is 50 bitcoins shifted right once per 210,000 blocks (GetBlockSubsidy): 625,000,000 satoshis before block 840,000 and 312,500,000 from it, as in block 971,489.

nodes.label: Fees versus subsidy
nodes.body: The book says in its section on fee sniping that the attack is not very lucrative today because the block subsidy is much higher than the total fees per block, and that at some point in the future fees will be the majority of the reward (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Whether that is true depends on the block. Block 840,000, mined on 2024-04-20, paid its miner 4,075,061,499 satoshis of which 3,762,561,499 (37.6 bitcoins) were fees, only 312,500,000 (3.125 bitcoins) subsidy: the fees were 92.33 percent of the reward. Block 971,489 of 2026-10-15 carried fees of 1,454,221 satoshis against the same subsidy, 0.46 percent (Mempool Space, 2026). It is like the tips of a restaurant, which on one evening can be larger than the wage and on another a few coins. The statement of the book is a fair description of an average block and is wrong for the halving block, a correction that the chapter lists among its findings; the share is computed here from the explorer's numbers and the rule of the subsidy (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: A future with fees only
nodes.body: Satoshi Nakamoto's paper says that the incentive for miners can also be funded with transaction fees: if the output value of a transaction is less than its input value, the difference is a transaction fee that is added to the incentive value of the block, and once a predetermined number of coins have entered circulation the incentive can transition entirely to fees (Nakamoto, 2008). The book follows this line when it says that the fees become more and more important as the subsidy declines and provide the incentive to continue securing Bitcoin with proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Carlsten and his coauthors at Princeton asked whether it makes no difference to security whether miners are paid by block rewards or by fees, and showed that it does: with only fees the variance of the reward grows and new strategies appear (Carlsten et al., 2016). It is like a shop that is paid only by tips and not by a wage. The chapter finds both passages in its saved copies of the papers and does not simulate their models; the question is open in the sense that it depends on the future of the fee market. This example reads carlsten_2016_instability.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. nodes.definition: Satoshi Nakamoto's paper says transaction fees can fund the incentive once the coins are all in circulation, and a 2016 Princeton paper argues that a fee-only chain is less stable; both passages are found in the saved copies, and neither is recomputed.

nodes.label: Sniping attack
nodes.body: This subject asks how likely and how dangerous fee sniping is: the formula of its chance and the undercutting attack of the Princeton study (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It matters because the book calls the attack theoretical, and the numbers show how the chance rises with the hash rate. This subject covers Sniping probability; Undercutting attack.

nodes.label: Sniping probability
nodes.body: Fee sniping is the attack in which a miner deliberately re-mines one or more earlier blocks to take the fees from the miners who first created them, perhaps with a block extending the chain at the same time; the Optech topic page gives the dishonest miner's chance of success, if every other miner is honest, as (x / (1 - x)) squared, where x is the miner's share of the hash rate (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). The formula is small but telling: a miner with a tenth of the hash rate succeeds with probability 1.23 percent, one with 30 percent with 18.37 percent, one with 45 percent with 66.94 percent, and one with half with certainty, since a miner who can out-mine all others combined can always win the race. It is like a race in which the cheat has to run two laps while the honest runners run one. The chapter computed the values with the formula and does not claim that real miners do this; the book calls it a theoretical attack scenario and the hash rate of single miners is below the levels where the chance is high (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A miner with a share x of the hash rate wins the race to re-mine the last block and extend it with probability (x / (1 - x)) squared: 1.23 percent for 10 percent, 18.37 percent for 30 percent and 66.94 percent for 45 percent, reaching certainty at one half.

nodes.label: Undercutting attack
nodes.body: In the study On the Instability of Bitcoin Without the Block Reward, Carlsten, Kalodner, Weinberg and Narayanan from Princeton University show that when transaction fees are the only reward, mining honestly may no longer be the best strategy; a miner can profit by forking the head of the chain and leaving the high-fee transactions of the latest block unmined, so that the next blocks collect them, which they call the undercutting attack (Carlsten et al., 2016). It is like a bakery that waits for the neighbour's best bread to be taken away and sells it as its own. The paper's simulator explores strategies and finds that undercutting can be harmful to the stability of Bitcoin consensus, and the authors conclude that the role of block rewards must be rethought. The chapter found the passages in the saved copy of the paper, which is dated 2016 and was presented at the ACM conference on computer and communications security in Vienna; it did not rerun the simulator, and it reports the paper as a reason for the defence in the next leaves (Carlsten et al., 2016). This example reads carlsten_2016_instability.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. nodes.label: Lock time defense against fee sniping
nodes.body: This subject asks how a wallet defends against fee sniping with the lock time: the rule of Bitcoin Core, its fallback, the use on the real chain, the exact boundary of the consensus rule, the effect of the final sequence and the proposal for taproot (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It matters because the book's example is off by one block, and the correct rule is the one the node enforces. This subject covers Wallet lock time rule; Wallet lag fallback; Share of mainnet transactions with the previous height; Lock time boundary; Final sequence disables lock time; Taproot anti-fee-sniping (BIP 326).

nodes.label: Wallet lock time rule
nodes.body: A lock time is a field of the transaction that says in which block height or at which time the transaction becomes valid. To discourage fee sniping a wallet sets it to the height of the current tip, so that only the next block can include the transaction; the source comment says that a miner who considers fee sniping then has fewer options for pulling off the attack (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In about one case in ten the code subtracts a random number of 0 to 99 blocks, which is good for the privacy of transactions that are broadcast late. The run made 60 payments with the wallet and read their lock times: 56 equal the tip and four were back-dated, by 6, 28, 35 and 54 blocks, all below 100; every one carried the sequence 0xfffffffd. The expected share is 10 percent and the run gave 6.7 percent, which is within the chance of a sample so small. It is like a date stamp that says not before today. The book recommends this defence for all wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The wallet sets the lock time to the height of the tip, and in about one case in ten back-dates it by a random 0 to 99 blocks: 56 of 60 transactions in the run had the tip, four were back-dated by 6, 28, 35 and 54.

nodes.label: Wallet lag fallback
nodes.body: The defence only makes sense if the wallet knows the real tip. The source of the wallet defines the function IsCurrentForAntiFeeSniping, which returns false while the node is in initial block download or when the best block is older than 8 hours, a constant MAX_ANTI_FEE_SNIPING_TIP_AGE of 8 x 60 x 60 seconds (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In that case the code sets the lock time to a constant 0, with the comment that this avoids leaking a potentially unique lock time fingerprint, since a wallet with an old tip would write an old height that others do not. It is like a clerk who does not write the date on a form when the office calendar is out of date. The chapter found the constant and the two statements in the saved source and computed 8 x 60 x 60 = 28,800 seconds; the case was not run, because a regtest chain made on the same day is never older than eight hours and the test would only show the same value 0.
nodes.example: a tip older than 8 hours means lock time 0
nodes.definition: When the node is still syncing or its tip is older than 8 hours the wallet sets the lock time to 0, so as not to leak a unique fingerprint.

nodes.label: Share of mainnet transactions with the previous height
nodes.body: Do real wallets use the defence? The chapter counted, in the first 599 transactions after the coinbase of two mainnet blocks, how many carry a lock time equal to the height of the previous block, which is what a wallet that follows the rule writes when the transaction is created while that block is the tip. In block 840,000 (2024-04-20) it was 89 of 599 (15 percent) and in block 971,489 (2026-10-15) 33 of 599 (6 percent); a lock time of 0 was carried by 507 and 563 (Mempool Space, 2026). The share is a lower bound for wallets that follow the rule, because a transaction created some blocks earlier will show an older height, and an upper bound for nothing in particular, because other software may write the same number. It is like counting how many cars have their lights on at noon. The defence is therefore used but not general (Bitcoin Optech, 2026), and BIP 326 mentions that about a fifth of recent transactions had anti-fee-sniping lock times in the author's data (Belcher, 2021).

nodes.label: Lock time boundary
nodes.body: The book sets the lock time of the example to 100,001 when the highest block is 100,000 and says that the transaction can only be included in block 100,001, the next block; the chapter on transactions says that a lock time of 123,456 can be included in block 123,456 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The consensus rule in the function IsFinalTx is different by one: a transaction with a lock time below the height of the block is final, so a lock time equal to the height is not, and the earliest block for a lock time of L is the block L + 1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026); BIP 113 says the same in other words, that a transaction is excluded while the block height is less than or equal to the lock time (Kerin, 2015). The chapter computed the function for 100,001 in block 100,001 (not final) and for 100,000 (final), and ran it: with the tip at 129 a lock time of 130 was refused as non-final by the mempool and a block of height 130 containing it was rejected with bad-txns-nonfinal, while a lock time of 129 was accepted and mined; the wallet, in the run above, used the tip. It is like a ticket that is valid from the day after the date printed on it. This is an error of the printed book, and it is not corrected on the development branch.
nodes.definition: A transaction is final in a block when its lock time is below the block's height, so a lock time equal to the height is not: on the node a lock time of the next block's height was refused as non-final and rejected from a block, and the tip's height was accepted.

nodes.label: Final sequence disables lock time
nodes.body: A lock time is only enforced when at least one input of the transaction has a sequence number that is not final; if every input has the sequence 0xffffffff, the transaction is final whatever its lock time says, and the function IsFinalTx returns true after its loop over the inputs (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's chapter on transactions describes the same: setting the sequence to its maximum value finalizes the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like an agreement in which a special clause overrides the date. In the run, at the tip 254, a transaction with the lock time 255 and the sequence 0xffffffff was accepted by the mempool, the same transaction with the sequence 0xfffffffd was refused as non-final, the one with lock time equal to the tip was accepted, and after one block (tip 255) the transaction with 255 and 0xfffffffd became acceptable. This is why a wallet that wants the defence against fee sniping must never use the final sequence, and the source asserts it, in the code that sets the lock time (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: A lock time is ignored when every input has the final sequence 0xffffffff, so a lock time of tip plus 1 was accepted with that sequence and refused with 0xfffffffd, and the same transaction became acceptable one block later.

nodes.label: Taproot anti-fee-sniping (BIP 326)
nodes.body: The lock time field has a disadvantage: it is used by few wallets for other reasons, so it can reveal which software made a transaction. BIP 326 proposes that wallets set the sequence field in their taproot transactions, in place of their regular lock time protection, so that a transaction with a sequence value is not unusual and the anti-fee-sniping protection also works for those who use the sequence of BIP 68 (Belcher, 2021). It argues that with the protection by lock time or sequence the bad miner soon runs out of transactions to put in the first block and has to change the plan. It is like using a stamp that many people use so that the letter does not stand out. The proposal is for taproot outputs, which the book discusses in other chapters, and it keeps the lock time as well in some transactions, because absolute lock times are still used. The chapter found the passages in the saved copy of the BIP and did not execute the proposal, because Bitcoin Core 31.1 was not shown to implement it.

findings: Background

The chapter holds that a transaction carries no fee field and that the fee is the difference between the inputs and the outputs, paid by the spender and collected by the miner of the block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A parse of the raw bytes of a transaction of the Bitcoin Core 31.1 test chain found version, inputs, outputs and lock time and no fee, and a forgotten change output of a 20-bitcoin input made the node refuse the transaction with max-fee-exceeded (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Background

The chapter states that the fee is a bid for room in a block, the idea that the original paper already described as an incentive that replaces the subsidy over time (Nakamoto, 2008). A block template of the test node listed ten transactions in descending order of fee rate, from 50 to 1 satoshi per virtual byte (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Background

The fee market is an economic subject with an early literature: fees depend on size and priority, and a fee market can exist without a block size limit (Moeser and Boehme, 2015); (Rizun, 2015). The chapter is consistent with it, since the chapter ties the fee to the block space a transaction takes up (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Erratum: the book's remark that the block subsidy is much higher than the fees is true of some blocks and not of others. In block 840,000, the halving block of 2024-04-20, the fees were 3,762,561,499 satoshis, 92.33 percent of the reward, while in block 971,489 they were 0.46 percent (Mempool Space, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Erratum: the book's summary of the default mempool as about one day's worth of transactions does not match the code, which holds 300 megabytes and forgets a transaction after 336 hours, 14 days; and the glossary's minimum fee of 0.5 millibitcoin, 50,000 satoshis, is a historical value that the node no longer applies (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The estimatesmartfee call accepts a target of 1 to 1008 blocks but can look back only as far as its history; on a chain 231 blocks high the target of 144 was answered for 60 blocks, and the default mode has been economical since 28.0, so that the default answer differs from the conservative one at 144 blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024).
Comparative analysis

The replacement hazards are real and measured: three versions of one payment of 0.4 bitcoin made the payee receive 0.8 bitcoin when a miner kept the first and then mined the last, and a large child pins a parent at a cost of 450,780 satoshis to replace. The replacement cycling attack of 2023 is described in the sources but was not run (Bitcoin Optech, 2023); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The incentive question of the last section is modelled by Carlsten and colleagues, who show that a chain without a subsidy is unstable because a miner gains by undercutting the block of a rival (Narayanan, 2016), and the probability that a miner with the hash share x wins a sniping race is (x / (1 - x)) squared: 1.23 percent at 10 percent, 66.94 percent at 45 percent (Carlsten et al., 2016); (Poon and Dryja, 2016).
Conclusion

Erratum: the lock time rule of the book and its chapter 6 is off by one: a transaction is final in a block when its lock time is less than the block height, so a lock time equal to the height of the next block is refused on the node. The wallet sets the lock time to the current height, which 89 of 599 transactions of block 840,000 do (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Kerin, 2015); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Conclusion

Taken together, the chapter's teaching on fees, replacement, child-pays-for-parent and anti-sniping remains right in its principles, but five of its defaults and limits are outdated for Bitcoin Core 28 to 31, and the sources show the direction: policy is moving from fixed limits and opt-in signals to cluster-based rules, TRUC transactions and anchors (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Conclusion

Bitcoin Core's own documentation describes the replacement rules in force, including an incremental relay fee of 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte, so a replacement of a 141-byte transaction that had paid 564 satoshis needed at least 579 satoshis in the run (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Harding, 2015).
Contemporary developments

Erratum: the book defines the fee rate as a transaction's size divided by weight, which is a pure number with no price in it. The fee rate is the fee divided by the size, 2.0 satoshis per virtual byte for the run's 141-byte transaction that paid 282 satoshis, whereas size over weight is 0.2513 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Lombrozo et al., 2015).
Contemporary developments

Changed default: the minimum relay fee rate fell from 1 to 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte in Bitcoin Core 30.0, so that the node accepted 15 satoshis for a 141-byte transaction and refused 14, while the wallet keeps its own minimum of 1 satoshi per virtual byte and refused 0.5 and 0.1 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed default: full replace-by-fee is the default since Bitcoin Core 28.0, so a transaction that does not signal replaceability is replaced on the 31.1 node, and the option -mempoolfullrbf was removed in 29.0 and is refused by 31.1 with exit code 1. The book describes only the opt-in rule of BIP 125 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Harding, 2015).
Contemporary developments

The change of the default followed a public discussion in December 2022 in which Peter Todd posted on full replace-by-fee on 2022-12-12 and release 24.0.1 announced the option -mempoolfullrbf (Todd, 2022); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2022); (Bitcoin Optech, 2022).
Contemporary developments

Package relay is partly realized: Bitcoin Core 28.0 accepts a package of one parent and one child through submitpackage, so that a child can pay for a parent that is below the minimum relay fee (the test node took a parent of 0 fee and a child of 10,000 satoshis), while the peer-to-peer ancestor package relay of BIP 331 is still a Draft (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024); (Zhao, 2022).
Contemporary developments

Erratum: the book gives the extra child of the CPFP carve-out as 1,000 virtual bytes and the limit as 100,000, while the code constant EXTRA_DESCENDANT_TX_SIZE_LIMIT is 10,000 and the descendant size limit is 101,000; the carve-out was added in release 0.19.0.1, not 0.19.0, which was tagged and never released (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2019); (Corallo, 2018).
Contemporary developments

Changed policy: the cluster mempool of Bitcoin Core 31.0 replaces the 25-transaction ancestor and descendant limits by a limit of 64 transactions per cluster, and the carve-out of the old limits is removed, and the run shows the quadratic work of the old limits (625 package updates, and 2,500 at double the limit) (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026); (Daftuar et al., 2024).
Contemporary developments

Version-3 (TRUC) transactions of Bitcoin Core 28.0 limit a transaction to one unconfirmed parent and one child, at most 10,000 virtual bytes for the transaction and 1,000 for the child. In the run the cost of replacing a pinned parent fell from 450,780 to 5,145 satoshis, 88 times less than for an unrestricted large child (Zhao, 2024); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Anchor outputs gained a standard form: the pay-to-anchor output script 51024e73 of BIP 433 can be spent by anyone, and release 29.0 relays a zero-fee parent with an ephemeral dust output when a child spends the dust in the same package. The lightning anchor commitments of BOLT 3 are the application the chapter names (Sanders, 2025); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Lightning developers, 2026).

stories.title: A node that only listens to replacements
stories.who: Peter Todd, a Bitcoin developer who posted the build, and Antoine Riard, whose peering code it contains
stories.where: the bitcoin-dev mailing list, and the nodes of the public Bitcoin network that run Bitcoin Core 24.0.1
stories.story: On Monday 12 December 2022 Peter Todd posted to the bitcoin-dev list a build of Bitcoin Core 24.0.1 with Antoine Riard's full-rbf peering code. Release 24.0.1 had just added the option mempoolfullrbf, which defaults to off and so allows only opt-in replacement. Todd's build advertises a FULL_RBF service bit when the option is set and connects to four additional nodes that do the same, so that a core group of nodes passes on replacements reliably. He estimated about 30 reliable nodes running his branch and about 50 Bitcoin Knots nodes that advertised the bit. Bitcoin Optech's newsletter of 14 December 2022 reported the monitoring of full-rbf replacements, and Bitcoin Core 28.0 later made full replacement the default and 29.0 removed the option. The test node of this chapter accepts a replacement of a transaction that never signalled.
stories.lesson: Policy is what most nodes choose to relay, and it changes by their choice

stories.title: A pre-signed transaction cannot guess next week's fee
stories.who: Matt Corallo, a Bitcoin Core and Lightning developer, writing to the bitcoin-dev and lightning-dev lists
stories.where: the bitcoin-dev and lightning-dev mailing lists, cross-posted; the rule shipped in Bitcoin Core 0.19.0.1
stories.story: On Thursday 29 November 2018 Matt Corallo wrote that Lightning channels exchange pre-signed transactions that are broadcast much later, so their fee has to be predicted or added afterwards by a child. He described how a counterparty could chain a large child of only moderate fee rate to the anyone-can-spend output of a commitment transaction and keep it at the bottom of the mempool. His answer, the carve-out, allowed one extra small child beyond the usual limits, and he proposed that it be no greater than 1K in virtual size. Bitcoin Core 0.19.0.1 shipped the carve-out in November 2019 with an extra child of up to 10,000 virtual bytes, and Bitcoin Core 31.0 removed it with the cluster mempool. The book states 1,000 and 100,000 where the code says 10,000 and 101,000.
stories.lesson: A limit built for one attack can outlive the problem it solved

stories.title: The block in which fees were nearly the whole reward
stories.who: the mining pool ViaBTC, which found block 840,000, and the Bitcoin Core rule that halves the subsidy every 210,000 blocks
stories.where: the Bitcoin chain at height 840,000, the block of the fourth halving
stories.story: Block 840,000 was found on 20 April 2024 at 00:09 UTC by the pool ViaBTC and held 3,050 transactions. It was the first block after the fourth halving, so the subsidy fell from 6.25 to 3.125 bitcoins, 312,500,000 satoshis. The fees in the same block were 3,762,561,499 satoshis, so the reward of 4,075,061,499 satoshis was 92.33 percent fees. In block 971,489 the fees were only 0.46 percent of the reward. The book says that the subsidy is much higher than the fees, which is true of that later block and false of the halving block.

stories.title: What if nobody got a subsidy?
stories.who: Miles Carlsten, Harry Kalodner, S. Matthew Weinberg and Arvind Narayanan, computer scientists at Princeton University
stories.where: Princeton University, New Jersey; the paper was presented at ACM CCS, the week after the announcement
stories.story: On 21 October 2016 Arvind Narayanan announced on the Princeton CITP blog the paper On the Instability of Bitcoin Without the Block Reward, written with Miles Carlsten, Harry Kalodner and Matt Weinberg and presented at ACM CCS the next week. They start from the observation that Bitcoin gives miners two incentives, block rewards and transaction fees, and that the first is expected to give way to the second. Their model shows that when fees are the main income a miner can gain by undercutting a block of a rival, which makes mining less stable. The chapter's last section describes the same pressure as fee sniping, and the run computes that a miner with 45 percent of the hash rate wins the race to re-mine a block with probability 66.94 percent. The wallet's countermeasure is the lock time of the current height.
stories.lesson: Fees must replace the subsidy, so the rules for fees must be stable

lecture.title: Chapter 9: Transaction Fees
lecture.say: This deck explains transaction fees: who pays them, how they are priced, how a payment is replaced or bumped, and what has changed since the book went to print. Every example runs under Python 3.14.6 on the chapter's own library, and Bitcoin Core 31.1 was run on a test network, so its answers are Recorded and only read back here. The research package for chapter 9 holds the sources and the claims.
lecture.takeaway: Who pays a fee, how it is priced, replaced and bumped, and what moved since print. Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are Recorded.

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: The route has four parts after the questions: what a fee is and how it is priced, estimating fees and reading the market, replacing and bumping a transaction, and finally pinning, anchors, clusters and sniping. Each part carries a true story or a correction of the book that a reader can check on the slide. The numbers in the list let a reader jump straight to a part.
lecture.takeaway: Four parts, four true stories, and a list of what was not run

lecture.title: The questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: The chapter asks two questions that this deck answers by computation: which of its statements can be checked, and what has changed since print. The three numbers are counted from the research package, which holds 72 sources, 20 findings and 71 executed claims. Each slide that follows shows the computation behind one claim.
lecture.takeaway: Its own competency questions, and the numbers behind the answers

lecture.title: Who pays, and how a fee is priced
lecture.say: This part starts from the simplest fact, that a fee is the difference between inputs and outputs, and prices it in virtual bytes. It ends with the floors that nodes and wallets apply, and with the dust rule that bars tiny outputs. Each slide has a console that ran on the test node of Bitcoin Core 31.1.
lecture.takeaway: A fee is what is left over; size is counted in virtual bytes, and nodes and wallets set a floor.

lecture.title: A fee is a difference, not a field
lecture.say: A Bitcoin transaction has no fee field: the fee is what the inputs hold minus what the outputs take, and the miner of the block collects it. The console parses the raw bytes of a test transaction and finds only version, inputs, outputs and lock time. Core refused a transaction that forgot its change, because 19 bitcoins would have gone to the miner. Lowering an output after signing breaks the signature, so only the spender can set the fee.
lecture.takeaway: The fee exists only as inputs minus outputs, so only the signer can set it

lecture.title: Virtual size and the fee rate
lecture.say: Weight counts witness bytes once and other bytes four times, and the virtual size is the weight divided by four, rounded up. The console parses a test transaction and finds 113 bytes without witness, 222 with it, weight 561 and 141 virtual bytes. The fee rate is the fee divided by the virtual size, 2.0 satoshis per virtual byte here, whereas the book's size divided by weight is a pure number. The unit of estimatesmartfee is bitcoin per kilovirtual byte.
lecture.takeaway: The fee rate is the fee over virtual size; size over weight is no price

lecture.title: Minimum fees and dust
lecture.say: A node refuses a transaction below its minimum relay fee: since Bitcoin Core 30.0 that is 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte, so a 141-byte transaction needs 15 satoshis and the node refused 8 and 14. Bitcoin Core's wallet keeps its own minimum of 1 satoshi per virtual byte, ten times higher. An output is dust when it costs more to spend than it is worth: 294 satoshis for P2WPKH, 330 for P2WSH and 240 for pay to anchor.
lecture.takeaway: The node floor is 0.1 sat/vB; the wallet floor is ten times higher

lecture.title: Estimating fees, and the market
lecture.say: This part asks how a wallet guesses a good fee and what the market for block space looked like in two real blocks. The bus on the slide is the picture to keep: a block is a bus with a fixed number of seats, and a fee is a bid for one. The part ends with the story of the halving block, in which fees were almost the whole reward.
lecture.takeaway: Like seats on a bus that leaves every ten minutes: the highest bids board first.

lecture.title: The estimator learns from blocks
lecture.say: The call estimatesmartfee looks for the lowest fee rate at which most recent transactions confirmed within the target, so it needs history. A fresh test node answered Insufficient data; after 120 blocks and 2,640 payments of mixed fee rates it answered 1.225 satoshis per virtual byte. The target of 144 blocks was answered for only 60, because the node's history was that long. Since Bitcoin Core 28.0 the default mode is economical, not conservative.
lecture.takeaway: The estimator needs history; a fresh node answers with no estimate

lecture.title: Two blocks, two fee markets
lecture.say: A census of the first 599 transactions after the coinbase of two real blocks shows how much the market moves. In the halving block of April 2024 the median fee rate was 1,436 satoshis per virtual byte and fees were 92.33 percent of the reward; in block 971,489, mined on 15 October 2026, the median was 3.02 and fees were 0.46 percent. The share of transactions that signal replaceability fell from 81 to 46 percent.
lecture.takeaway: Fees were 92.33 percent of the reward in 2024 and 0.46 percent in 2026

lecture.title: The block where fees were nearly the reward
lecture.say: On 20 April 2024 the pool ViaBTC found block 840,000, the first block after the fourth halving, which cut the subsidy to 312,500,000 satoshis. The fees in the same block were 3,762,561,499 satoshis, so the reward of 4,075,061,499 was 92.33 percent fees. In block 971,489 the fees were only 0.46 percent. The book's remark that the subsidy is much higher than fees is true of some blocks and not of others.
lecture.takeaway: The story of 20 April 2024: who, where, when and what to read next

lecture.title: Replace, bump and relay
lecture.say: This part covers what a sender or a receiver can do when a transaction pays too little and waits. The sender can replace it with a better-paying version, and the receiver can add a child that pays for both. The story shows how the default changed from opt-in to full replacement, and the hazards slide shows what that costs.
lecture.takeaway: From replacing a payment to paying for a parent: what a wallet can do when the fee was set too low.

lecture.title: A replacement must pay more than it replaces
lecture.say: Replace by fee lets a sender swap a waiting transaction for another that spends the same output. The replacement must pay at least the absolute fee of what it replaces, plus the incremental relay fee for its own size. On the test node a replacement of 514 satoshis was refused for paying less, 564 for paying nothing extra, 578 by one satoshi, and 579 was accepted. A transaction signals replaceability when an input has a sequence below 0xfffffffe.
lecture.takeaway: A replacement pays more in total and pays for its own relay too

lecture.title: When replacement goes wrong
lecture.say: Three versions of one payment of 0.4 bitcoin conflict in a chain: version 1 replaces version 0, and version 2 conflicts with version 1 but not with version 0. A miner that kept version 0 mined it and then version 2, so the payee received 0.8 bitcoin. A large child also pins a parent: replacing a 705-satoshi parent cost 450,780 satoshis. The replacement cycling attack of 2023 is described in the sources but was not run.
lecture.takeaway: Replacement is a hazard as well as a tool, and here it was measured

lecture.title: Child pays for parent, and packages
lecture.say: A receiver can pay for a stuck parent by spending its output in a child with a high fee, because miners rank a transaction together with its unconfirmed ancestors. In the run a parent paying 141 satoshis and a child paying 14,100 formed a package at 50.77 satoshis per virtual byte, and the node mined the pair before an unrelated transaction at 20. A child at 5 satoshis per virtual byte did not help. The submitpackage call took a parent of 8 satoshis with its child.
lecture.takeaway: A child can pay for its parent when the pair's fee rate is high enough

lecture.title: Pinning, anchors, clusters, sniping
lecture.say: This part is about the attacks and fixes that came after the book's model of fees. A large child can pin a parent, and version 3 transactions, anchor outputs and the cluster mempool of Core 31.0 are the answers. The last slides turn to fee sniping and to the question of what happens when the subsidy is gone.
lecture.takeaway: How a child can pin a parent, and what version 3, anchors and clusters changed.

lecture.title: A large child can pin a parent
lecture.say: A counterparty can attach a very large child of modest fee rate to a payment, and then a replacement has to pay for the child too. In the run a child of 90,012 virtual bytes raised the price of replacing the parent to 450,780 satoshis. Version 3, the TRUC policy of Bitcoin Core 28.0, caps the child at 1,000 virtual bytes, and the same replacement cost 5,145 satoshis, 88 times less. A version-3 child of 1,350 bytes was refused.
lecture.takeaway: Version 3 caps the child, so replacing a pinned parent cost 88 times less

lecture.title: Anchors: a fee added afterwards
lecture.say: A pay-to-anchor output is a tiny output that anyone can spend, so whoever needs a transaction confirmed can attach a child and pay the fee then. In the run a version-3 parent paying nothing was refused alone with min relay fee not met, and accepted with its child through submitpackage at 36.5 satoshis per virtual byte. The child spent the anchor with an empty witness stack. Lightning commitment transactions use such anchors.
lecture.takeaway: An anchor lets whoever needs it add the fee after the transaction is signed

lecture.title: Pre-signed transactions cannot guess fees
lecture.say: On 29 November 2018 Matt Corallo wrote that Lightning channels exchange pre-signed transactions that are broadcast much later, so their fee must be predicted or added afterwards by a child. His answer, the carve-out, allowed one extra small child beyond the usual limits: he proposed 1K, and Bitcoin Core 0.19.0.1 shipped 10,000 virtual bytes where the book says 1,000. The removal in Core 31.0 was found in the saved notes and not run on an older node.
lecture.takeaway: The story of 29 November 2018: who, where, when and what to read next

lecture.title: Cluster mempool replaces the old limits
lecture.say: The old limits of 25 ancestors or descendants existed because updating them was quadratic: 25 children of 25 ancestors need 625 package updates, and doubling the limit makes 2,500. Release 31.0 replaces them with clusters of at most 64 transactions and 101,000 virtual bytes, and the carve-out is removed. The test node accepted a chain of 64 and refused the 65th. The mempool keeps 300 megabytes and forgets a transaction after 336 hours, 14 days, not one day.
lecture.takeaway: Cluster limits replaced the 25-transaction limits and removed the carve-out

lecture.title: Fee sniping and the lock time
lecture.say: A miner who could re-mine the last block and take its fees might tempt others to build on the older block. A wallet defends by setting the lock time to the current height, so that such a transaction cannot be placed in an older block; in the run 56 of 60 transactions had the tip and four were back-dated. A transaction is final in a block when its lock time is below the height, which the book's chapter 6 gets off by one. BIP 326 for taproot was not executed.
lecture.takeaway: A lock time at the tip makes re-mining the last block pay less

lecture.title: What if nobody got a subsidy?
lecture.say: On 21 October 2016 Arvind Narayanan announced a Princeton paper, written with Miles Carlsten, Harry Kalodner and Matt Weinberg, on the instability of Bitcoin without the block reward. Satoshi Nakamoto's paper had already said that fees can replace the subsidy. The authors show that when fees are the main income a miner can gain by undercutting a rival's block. The model was not recomputed here; the passages were found in the saved copies.
